snippets.title: Wallet transaction search
snippets.context: A Lagos mobile money app lets customers search their own transaction history by narration, for example "airtime" or "POS withdrawal".
code: const sql = 'SELECT id, amount_kobo, narration, created_at FROM transactions ' +
snippets.explanation: The narration search term is pasted straight into the SQL text. A search for  x' OR 1=1 --  closes the quote, adds a condition that is always true and comments out the rest, so one customer can read every customer's transactions. The user_id on the same query is passed safely as $1; the narration is not.

fix.summary: Send the search term as a bound parameter ($2) and put the % wildcards in the value, never in the SQL string.
code: const sql = 'SELECT id, amount_kobo, narration, created_at FROM transactions ' +

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.9: String() only makes the value text; it doesn't make it safe. The danger is where that text is pasted into the SQL.
lineNotes.13: The user ID is passed as a parameter here, which is safe. The search text was already glued into the SQL above.

snippets.title: Results portal session filter
snippets.context: A university results portal. Signed-in students choose an academic session to see their grades for that year.
code: require 'session_guard.php'; // sets $studentId from the login session
'SELECT course_code, grade FROM results WHERE student_id = ? AND session = ?'
snippets.explanation: The session value from the URL is printed into the page with no encoding. A link like ?session=<script>...</script> shared in a class WhatsApp group runs script in every student's browser on the portal's own domain, where it can read their page, change what they see or send their session away. The table cells are escaped correctly; the heading is the one place that was missed.

fix.summary: Encode every value on output with htmlspecialchars, and reject session values that don't match the YYYY/YYYY format.
code: require 'session_guard.php'; // sets $studentId from the login session
'SELECT course_code, grade FROM results WHERE student_id = ? AND session = ?'
Your results for the session

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.9: The session is passed to the database as a parameter, so the query is safe. The problem is printing it on the page.
lineNotes.16: The course code is escaped with htmlspecialchars, so it's safe to print.

snippets.title: POS agent settlements
snippets.context: An API for a POS agent network. Agents open the app to check the daily settlements paid into their bank account.
code: from flask import Flask, jsonify, g
from auth import login_required  # sets g.agent for the signed-in agent
return jsonify([row.to_dict() for row in rows])
snippets.explanation: The query trusts the agent_id in the URL. Any signed-in agent can change /agents/1042/settlements to /agents/1043/settlements and read another agent's payouts and bank details. Logging in proves who you are; it doesn't prove which records you may see. This pattern is called IDOR, an insecure direct object reference.

fix.summary: Compare the requested ID with the signed-in agent (or drop the ID from the URL and use g.agent.id), and return 404 so other agents' IDs aren't confirmed.
code: from flask import Flask, jsonify, g, abort
from auth import login_required  # sets g.agent for the signed-in agent
return jsonify([row.to_dict() for row in rows])

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.9: Sign-in is required, but signing in only proves who you are. It doesn't check that the agent ID in the address is yours.

snippets.title: Card payment verification
snippets.context: Before a fintech app credits a customer's wallet, it asks the payment gateway to confirm the card payment really happened.
code: // Confirm a card payment before we credit the customer's wallet.
snippets.explanation: A live payment gateway secret is written into the source file. Everyone with repo access, every laptop that clones it and every old commit now holds a key that can act as your business on the gateway: list customers, query transactions or start refunds. Deleting the line later doesn't remove it from git history, so a leaked key must be rotated.

fix.summary: Load the secret from the environment or a secrets manager, fail fast when it's missing, and rotate any key that was ever committed.
code: if (!GATEWAY_SECRET) throw new Error('GATEWAY_SECRET is not set');
// Confirm a card payment before we credit the customer's wallet.

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.10: Sending the secret in the Authorization header is how the gateway expects it. The problem is that the secret is written in the code.
lineNotes.14: This check is good: the status, amount and currency all have to match.

snippets.title: Portal password helper
snippets.context: The password module shared by a school results portal's login and password reset routes.
code: # Used by the results portal login and the password reset flow.
def verify_password(password: str, stored_hash: str) -> bool:
snippets.explanation: Passwords are stored as plain MD5. MD5 was designed to be fast and has no salt, so if the database leaks, one GPU can test billions of guesses a second, and two students with the same password get the same hash. The constant-time comparison at the bottom is good practice, but it can't make a weak hash strong.

fix.summary: Use a slow, salted password hashing function (scrypt, bcrypt or Argon2). Werkzeug, which ships with Flask, provides one.
code: # Used by the results portal login and the password reset flow.
return generate_password_hash(password)  # salted, slow, per-user hash
def verify_password(password: str, stored_hash: str) -> bool:

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.12: compare_digest is the right way to compare hashes. The weakness is the hash itself.

snippets.title: School fees receipt download
snippets.context: Students download PDF receipts for school fees they've paid. Each student has their own receipts folder on the server.
code: require 'session_guard.php'; // sets $studentId from the login session
// Each student has their own folder of school fees receipts.
snippets.explanation: The filename from the URL is joined onto the student's folder as is. A request for ?file=../../../config.php climbs out of the receipts folder and downloads the portal's config file, database password included, or another student's receipts. The folder is per student, but nothing stops the path from leaving it.

fix.summary: Strip directories with basename(), resolve the real path, and confirm it still sits inside the student's folder before reading it.
code: require 'session_guard.php'; // sets $studentId from the login session
// Each student has their own folder of school fees receipts.

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.5: The folder comes from the student's own ID in the session, which is fine. The file name from the address is the problem.

snippets.title: Merchant logo from a link
snippets.context: Merchants on a payments dashboard paste a link to their shop logo. The server downloads the image and keeps a copy.
code: // Merchants paste a link to their shop logo; we download and keep a copy.
if (!upstream.ok) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Could not fetch logo' });
snippets.explanation: The server fetches whatever URL the merchant sends. Point it at http://169.254.169.254/ (the cloud metadata service) or http://10.0.0.5:8080/admin and the request comes from inside your network, where firewalls trust it. The response is then saved as a "logo" the attacker can download.

fix.summary: Allow only https, resolve the hostname and refuse private or internal addresses, block redirects and cap the size. In production, pin the resolved IP or send outbound calls through an egress proxy.
code: // Merchants paste a link to their shop logo; we download and keep a copy.
return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Use a public https link' });
const upstream = await fetch(url, { timeout: 5000, redirect: 'error', size: 2e6 });
if (!upstream.ok) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Could not fetch logo' });

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.10: Reading the link from the request is normal. The danger is fetching it without checking where it points.
lineNotes.14: Saving the logo for the signed-in merchant is fine.

snippets.title: POS terminal preferences cookie
snippets.context: A POS terminal's companion app remembers the agent's language and receipt choice in a cookie.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
snippets.explanation: The server unpickles a cookie that the client fully controls. pickle can rebuild any Python object, including one whose __reduce__ method runs a shell command, so a single crafted cookie gives an attacker code execution on the server. Base64 is only encoding; it hides nothing and checks nothing.

fix.summary: Store plain data as JSON (or a signed session) and check the shape of what comes back. Never unpickle data from outside your trust boundary.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.10: Reading a cookie is normal. The problem is what's done with it next.

snippets.title: Wallet to wallet transfer
snippets.context: The transfer endpoint of a Nigerian fintech app. Amounts are sent in kobo (100 kobo = ₦1).
snippets.explanation: The amount is cast to an integer and used without any range check. A transfer of -500000 kobo sails past the "insufficient funds" test, because a negative number is always smaller than the balance, and moveFunds then debits the sender by a negative amount: ₦5,000 moves out of the recipient's wallet into the attacker's. The balance check looks like validation but only guards one direction.

fix.summary: Validate on the server before any money moves: a whole number of kobo within your minimum and maximum transfer limits, and a 10 digit NUBAN account number.
code: exit(json_encode(['error' => 'Enter a valid amount and a 10 digit account number']));

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.7: Removing everything but digits from the account number is a sensible clean-up.
lineNotes.11: Locking the wallet row stops two transfers from racing each other. That part is right.

snippets.title: API error handler
snippets.context: The POS agent API's last middleware. It catches any error a route throws and answers the client.
snippets.explanation: The error handler returns the raw error to whoever caused it: the message, the full stack trace with file paths and library versions, and the SQL that failed. Anyone can trigger an error with a malformed request and get a map of your code, tables and query shapes, which makes every other attack easier to aim. Logging the detail is right; sending it to the client is the bug.

fix.summary: Log the full error server side with a reference ID, and send the client a generic message plus that ID so support can find the log line.
code: logger.error({ err, ref, path: req.path }, 'request failed');
error: 'Something went wrong. Quote this reference if you contact support.',

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.10: Logging the full error on the server is fine and useful. The problem is sending it back to the caller.

snippets.title: POS agent app remembers the PIN
snippets.context: SparkPay's agent app signs POS agents in each morning. The session token goes into encrypted storage; the team also wanted agents to type less.
code: private val secureStore by lazy { SecureStore(this) }  // EncryptedSharedPreferences
private fun onLoginSuccess(agentId: String, pin: String, token: String) {
// Remember the agent so they don't retype everything each morning
snippets.explanation: SharedPreferences is a plain XML file in the app's data folder. Anyone with a rooted phone, a backup of it, or malware that gains root can open it and read the agent's PIN in plain text, and on a POS app that PIN approves cash outs. The token went into encrypted storage, but the PIN, which matters more, didn't.

private fun onLoginSuccess(agentId: String, pin: String, token: String) {
// Remember who the agent is, never their PIN: ask for it (or a fingerprint) each session

lineNotes.6: The session token goes into encrypted storage, which is right.
lineNotes.9: This file is private to the app but not encrypted. What matters is what gets written into it.

snippets.title: Wallet app that trusts any certificate
snippets.context: The SparkPay wallet's network client. A developer hit a certificate error while testing against a staging server last month.
snippets.explanation: Returning true from badCertificateCallback accepts every certificate, including one an attacker made five minutes ago. Anyone on the same Wi-Fi, hotspot or router can sit in the middle and read or change every request: sign in, PIN and transfers. The https:// in the URL no longer protects anything. It is usually added to get past a staging error and then shipped.

fix.summary: Remove the callback so normal certificate checks apply. Give staging a real certificate (for example from Let's Encrypt) instead of switching checks off.
code: ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 15);  // default certificate checks stay on

lineNotes.5: The base URL uses https, which is right. The client below then switches off the certificate check.
lineNotes.9: A connection timeout is only a time limit.

snippets.title: BVN check during account opening
snippets.context: New customers enter their 11-digit BVN and date of birth, and the app checks them with SparkPay's KYC API.
code: suspend fun verify(bvn: String, dateOfBirth: String): BvnResult {
require(bvn.length == 11 && bvn.all { it.isDigit() }) { "BVN must be 11 digits" }
snippets.explanation: Log.d is not removed from release builds unless you strip it. Every customer's BVN and date of birth goes to Logcat, where anyone with the phone and USB debugging can read it, and many crash and analytics tools collect recent logs. A BVN with a birth date is exactly what identity fraud needs. The failure log on the next lines is fine: it only records a status code.

fix.summary: Never log personal data. Log the event without the values, so the log tells you a check happened but not whose.

require(bvn.length == 11 && bvn.all { it.isDigit() }) { "BVN must be 11 digits" }
Log.d("KYC", "Verifying a BVN")  // never the BVN or date of birth

lineNotes.4: Checking the BVN is 11 digits is good validation.
lineNotes.8: This logs only the HTTP status code, which is safe.

snippets.title: Help pages opened from a link
snippets.context: Support agents send customers links like sparkpay://help?page=https://help.sparkpay.example/limits, which open help pages inside the app. The pages can show the wallet balance through a JavaScript bridge.
snippets.explanation: The app loads whatever address is in the link. A scammer sends sparkpay://help?page=https://their-site.example by SMS or WhatsApp, the app opens their page with JavaScript on, and the Wallet bridge is right there for their script to call. A help screen meant for trusted pages becomes a way into the wallet.

fix.summary: Only load pages from the help site over HTTPS, and fall back to the help home page for anything else.

lineNotes.8: Many help pages need JavaScript. On its own, that isn't the flaw.

snippets.title: Agent app screens in the manifest
snippets.context: The agent app: agents sign in, see their float, then confirm payouts after entering their PIN on the previous screen.
snippets.explanation: exported="true" lets any other app on the phone open the payout confirmation screen directly, with its own amount and account in the intent, skipping the sign in and the PIN step that normally come before it. Only the launcher screen needs to be exported; screens inside a flow should only be reachable from the app itself.

fix.summary: Set exported="false" on every screen that isn't an entry point. Inside the screen, also check that the agent is signed in and the PIN step was completed.

lineNotes.7: The launcher screen has to be exported so the phone can open the app.
lineNotes.16: Settings isn't exported, so other apps can't open it.

snippets.title: School results in Firestore
snippets.context: A secondary school's results app. Students sign in and read their own results; only the school's admin server writes them.
code: // Students read their own results after signing in
allow read: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == studentId;
allow write: if false;  // only the admin server writes results
snippets.explanation: Firestore rules add up: if any rule allows a request, it goes through. The careful results rule doesn't matter, because the catch-all at the bottom lets anyone, signed in or not, read and change every document, results included. It's what Firebase's "test mode" leaves behind if nobody removes it.

fix.summary: Delete the catch-all. Anything without its own rule is then denied by default.
code: // Students read their own results after signing in
allow read: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == studentId;
allow write: if false;  // only the admin server writes results
// No catch-all: anything without a rule above is denied

lineNotes.7: This rule is right: a student can read only their own results.
lineNotes.8: Nobody can write results from an app. That's safe.

snippets.title: Results portal container image
snippets.context: The school portal's API image is built on every release and pushed to the team's Docker Hub repository, where the hosting server pulls it.
snippets.explanation: The .env file, with the database password and payment keys, is copied into the image. Every copy of the image now carries it: anyone who can pull from the registry (everyone, if the repository is public), anyone with access to a server it ran on, and every old image tag you forgot to delete. Changing the .env later doesn't remove it from images already pushed.

fix.summary: Keep secrets out of the image. Pass them when the container starts (docker run --env-file, or your host's secret settings), and list .env in .dockerignore. Then rotate the keys that were exposed.
code: # Secrets come from the environment at run time (docker run --env-file .env), never the image

lineNotes.5: npm ci with --omit=dev installs exactly what's locked, without dev tools. Good practice.
lineNotes.11: Running as the node user instead of root is good.

snippets.title: Installing a PDF tool in CI
snippets.context: The receipts service needs a PDF tool for its tests, so a developer added the install command from the tool's website to the CI workflow.
snippets.explanation: The workflow downloads a script over plain http and runs it as root without looking at it. Whoever controls that website, or anyone who can tamper with the connection, decides what runs in your CI on every push. If they change the script tomorrow, your next build runs their code, with access to your source and anything the job can reach.

fix.summary: Install from a trusted, signed package source, or download one fixed release over HTTPS and check its published SHA-256 before running it.
code: - name: Install the PDF tool (signed package from the Ubuntu archive)
run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils

lineNotes.8: The job's token can only read the repository. Good.
lineNotes.13: npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says. That's fine.

snippets.title: Report worker in Docker Compose
snippets.context: The worker turns uploaded bank statements into PDF reports and saves them to the reports folder.
snippets.explanation: privileged: true gives the container nearly every power the host has, including its devices. The report worker opens files customers upload, so a bug in its PDF library is likely one day; with privileged mode, that bug becomes control of the whole server and every other container on it. Writing to one folder needs none of this.

fix.summary: Remove privileged. Run the worker as a normal user, drop all extra capabilities and make its file system read only apart from the reports folder.

lineNotes.6: Compose reads .env when it starts the container; it isn't baked into an image. That's fine.
lineNotes.17: The database password comes from a secret file, which is the safe way.

snippets.title: Results portal web server
snippets.context: The college's results portal. A nightly job saves a database dump to the backups folder, and the admin wanted to download them from a browser.
snippets.explanation: The backups folder is served to the whole internet, and autoindex even lists the files. Anyone who tries /backups/ (scanners do, constantly) can download every nightly dump: every student's results, phone numbers and the staff password hashes. There is no sign in in front of it at all.

fix.summary: Don't serve backups from the web server. Keep them outside the web root (better, on separate storage) and fetch them over SSH or an authenticated admin tool.
